sets.title: Community gardens
text: Many cities are now encouraging residents to take {{1}} in community gardening projects. These schemes allow neighbours to share a piece of land and grow vegetables together.

Whether the project works well often depends {{2}} how much free time the volunteers have. Most people who join agree to {{3}} after a small plot every weekend, watering the plants and pulling out weeds.
{{4}}, not everyone can help every single week, so groups usually share the jobs between several families. {{5}} harvest festival is held every September to celebrate the work of the whole year.

Community gardens are becoming {{6}} popular than private allotments because they cost less and bring people together. Everyone who joins {{7}} bring their own gloves and a small spade. In most neighbourhoods the festival {{8}} organised entirely by local volunteers, with no help from the city council.

why: 'Take piece' is not a real English collocation.
'Take place' means 'to happen', which does not fit here.
Correct: 'take part in' is a fixed collocation meaning 'to join in an activity'.
'Take role' is not a natural collocation; the usual phrase is 'play a role'.
Correct: the verb 'depend' is followed by the preposition 'on'.
'Depend of' is not correct in English.
'Depend for' is not correct in English.
'Depend with' is not correct in English.
Correct: 'look after' is a phrasal verb meaning 'to take care of'.
'Take after' means 'to resemble a relative', which does not fit here.
'Keep after' is not a standard English phrasal verb.
'Hold after' is not a standard English phrasal verb.
'Moreover' adds a similar point, but this sentence introduces a contrast.
Correct: 'However' signals the contrast between wanting to help and not always having time.
'Therefore' shows a result, which does not fit the contrast here.
'Besides' introduces an additional point, not a contrast.
'An' is used before vowel sounds and is also the wrong article here.
Correct: 'The' is used because the festival is a specific, well-known yearly event for this group.
'Some' is used for unspecified quantities, not a single specific event.
'A' would suggest one of several unspecified festivals, which does not fit.
'Very' cannot be followed by 'than'.
'Most popular' would need 'the' and does not fit the comparative structure with 'than'.
Correct: 'more...than' is the comparative form used to compare two things.
'Much' cannot directly replace a comparative adjective before 'than' like this.
'Might' expresses possibility, not obligation.
'Can' expresses ability or permission, not a required rule here.
'Would' does not express obligation in this context.
Correct: 'must' expresses the strong obligation that everyone needs their own gloves and spade.
'Was organised' is past tense, which does not match the present-tense description of a regular event.
'Has organised' would need 'been' to form a passive, and the meaning would still not fit.
'Does organised' is not a grammatically correct form.
Correct: the present simple passive 'is organised' fits because this happens every year, as already described.
